summary: Provides a framework for Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP), which supports the discovery and exchange of IP telephony gateway routing tables between providers. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: Phone companies need to tell each other which numbers they can reach. This describes the plan for sharing those lists across the Internet.

subtitle: A framework for letting telephony providers exchange routing tables for IP-to-phone gateways.

tldr.problem: Choosing which IP telephony gateway should complete a call to an ordinary phone number depends on business deals and policy, so no single global directory of gateways can work.
tldr.mechanism: Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP) has Location Servers in each administrative domain exchange gateway routes with their peers, applying policy and aggregating ranges of phone numbers, much like an application-layer cousin of BGP.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a framework only. It defines terms, architecture and the protocol's role, and leaves the protocol details to a separate TRIP specification.

facts.label: Routing object content
facts.value: Phone number range plus next-hop address

today: RFC 2871 is an Informational framework, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The protocol details are left to a separate TRIP specification.

sections.title: The Gateway Selection Problem
sections.content:
When a calling device on an IP network wants to reach a phone number on the circuit switched telephone network, it must use a telephony gateway that converts media and signaling between the two. Many gateways could complete the call, and choosing one is hard. The RFC lists the complications: a very large number of candidate gateways, business relationships (owners usually charge and restrict use), provider policy, end user policy, gateway capacity, and protocol and feature compatibility.

Because selection is driven by policy and relationships, the RFC concludes there cannot be a global directory of gateways in which users look up phone numbers. Providers must exchange gateway information, subject to policy, and each builds its own local database, which differs from provider to provider. TRIP is the inter-domain protocol for that exchange. Its functions include establishing and maintaining peering relationships, exchanging and synchronizing gateway routes, preventing stable routing loops, propagating routes in a timely and scalable way, and defining the syntax and semantics of route data.
sections.eli5: Many doors lead to the old phone network, and each door has an owner with their own rules and prices. So each company keeps its own list of doors it may use, and they swap lists.

sections.title: What TRIP Does Not Solve, and BGP
sections.content:
The RFC separates three problems that all look like phone number to IP address translation. Only the first is TRIP's: finding a gateway that can complete a call to a phone number on a circuit switched network. The other two, finding the IP address of a host that has a phone number, and finding the IP terminal owned by the user of a phone number, are name to address problems better handled by directory protocols.

TRIP is called a close cousin of inter-domain routing protocols such as BGP, with important differences. TRIP runs at the application layer between servers that may be separated by many networks, while BGP runs between usually adjacent routers. TRIP describes routes to application layer devices, and its peers need not forward the signaling that uses the routes. TRIP does not aim at global connectivity: many small islands of TRIP connectivity are reasonable. And TRIP exchanges ranges of phone numbers, not IP prefixes.
sections.eli5: TRIP only answers one question: which door leads to this phone number. It is like a big road map system for phone calls, but it works between servers, not between road-building machines.

sections.title: Architecture and Elements
sections.content:
The architecture has Internet Telephony Administrative Domains (ITADs). An ITAD is the set of gateways and Location Servers under one administrative authority, and it has at least one Location Server (LS). It may have no gateways (a virtual provider), no end users (a wholesaler), or neither (a reseller that only aggregates and propagates routes). An ITAD need not be the same as an autonomous system.

The LS is the main entity. It keeps the Telephony Routing Information Base (TRIB), built from local gateways and remote gateways learned through TRIP, according to policy. The LS learns local gateways through an intra-domain protocol, which is out of scope. The RFC suggests SLP, SIP or H.323 registration, or LDAP as possibilities, and says an LS can also use static configuration.

Gateways have attributes: the range of phone numbers they serve (possibly with a cost token), capacity (number of ports and access link speed), and service type (signaling protocols, features, codecs, encryption). The philosophy of TRIP is to keep it simple and favor scalability over abundance of information, and its attribute set is extensible.
sections.eli5: Each company has a helper server that knows its own doors and learns about other companies' doors. Policy decides what the helper accepts and what it tells others.

sections.title: How Location Servers Exchange Routes
sections.content:
Location Servers talk over persistent associations set up administratively, normally when the two administrators have an agreement. LS's in the same ITAD are internal peers; those in different ITADs are external peers. TRIP defines the syntax and semantics of the messages but does not dictate any policy or the nature of the agreements.

The information exchanged is a set of routing objects. Each minimally holds a range of reachable telephone numbers and an IP address or host name that is the application-layer next hop toward a gateway for that range. An LS may aggregate objects, merging number ranges and replacing the address with its own, before propagating them. More attributes make aggregation harder, so there is a trade-off between aggregatability and verbosity.

The RFC gives a worked case: LS C learns of gateways A and B and advertises one combined range Z to peer D. Caller E asks D for a call to number T, D sees T in Z and forwards to C, and C forwards to A, which starts the call toward the telephone network. Capacity is carried as a static metric usable for load balancing. TRIP itself defines no pricing metric, but one can be defined as an extension.
sections.eli5: Servers swap lists like "I can reach numbers starting with these digits." They can combine small lists into one bigger list, so there is less to carry around.

sections.title: Uses, Front Ends and Number Translation
sections.content:
The RFC shows three example uses: a clearinghouse that sits between member providers, a confederation in which providers form a full mesh, and gateway wholesalers in a pyramid where large providers resell to smaller ones. TRIP does not dictate the shape of these relationships.

The front end is how the TRIB is exposed to signaling servers, end users and administrators. TRIP does not specify it. Candidates named include SLP, the Open Settlements Protocol, LDAP, a web page, or TRIP itself for full database synchronization. A signaling server acting as a proxy hides the LS from the caller, while direct end user access allows richer preferences.

The RFC also strongly discourages advertising special numbers such as freephone and LNP numbers through TRIP, since they may have only local meaning and can cause very suboptimal call paths. Such translations should happen before the LS is consulted, and how that is done is outside TRIP.
sections.eli5: Different kinds of companies can use the same list-swapping idea. Special numbers like free-call numbers should be turned into real numbers first, so the lists stay accurate.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The TRIP model assumes a level of trust between peer Location Servers. Incorrect routing information could misroute calls completely, enabling a significant denial of service attack that might spread to other ITADs. The RFC therefore says mutual authentication of peer LS's is critical and message integrity is required.

TRIP messages can reveal an ITAD's routing capabilities, which competitors might use to learn its topology and capacity, so encryption is also supported. End to end authentication is limited, because aggregation modifies routing objects: authentication can only run from the point of last aggregation to the receiving LS.
sections.eli5: If someone lies on the list, calls go to the wrong place. So servers must check who they are talking to, make sure messages are not changed, and can keep them secret.
